title: [Full Workshop] Reinforcement Learning, Kernels, Reasoning, Quantization & Agents — Daniel Han
talk_summary: A workshop on RL training (PPO/GRPO/RLVR), reward functions, and Unsloth's memory optimizations for fine-tuning open models.

takeaways.technique: Verifiable reward functions instead of LLM-judge-only scoring
takeaways.what_they_do: They replace a learned reward model with deterministic check functions (regex format checks, exact-match, distance-based numeric scoring, code execution) that output a number, and warn that pure LLM-as-judge reward degrades over time.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can use this as a reward and so this blue box the reward can be anything that you like. It just needs to output a number

takeaways.technique: Partial credit / graded scoring over binary pass-fail
takeaways.what_they_do: They show that distance-based or partial rewards (e.g. +0.5 for seeing a required keyword, scaled penalty for near-misses) teach faster than all-or-nothing scoring, and that format-only rewards are a trap.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if we see a keyword, we plus one... this essentially allows you to partially reward the model

takeaways.technique: Ignore format metrics, watch the outcome metric
takeaways.what_they_do: In RL logs most runs 'follow the format' without learning; they instruct looking only at the final correctness/reward columns, not the format columns.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Most RL training runs just follow the format and it doesn't actually learn. So the format columns are not important.

takeaways.technique: Share weights / colocate inference and training to cut memory
takeaways.what_they_do: Unsloth shares vLLM weights directly with the trainer and colocates inference and fine-tuning on one machine, avoiding a second copy of weights and inter-server communication.
takeaways.numbers: ~50% memory reduction from weight sharing; ~70% memory reduction overall claimed

takeaways.technique: Prime with a small SFT set before expecting autonomous behavior
takeaways.what_they_do: They show that starting RL from a raw base model yields zero reward forever; a tiny priming set (~118 rows) of good traces teaches the behavior first, then optimization works.
takeaways.numbers: ~118 rows used for priming; 7,000-row dataset available

takeaways.technique: High-temperature sampling for exploration, low for production
takeaways.what_they_do: They recommend temperature ~1.0-1.2 with min-p 0.1 to maximize output variability during exploration, and warn that temperature 0 gives identical outputs every time.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you set temperature to be zero you'll have the same answer every single time. So, definitely don't do that.
